name: Hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome
aliases: mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome hepatocerebral form

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders presenting with infantile liver failure and neurological involvement due to quantitative depletion of mitochondrial DNA
Commonly caused by mutations in DGUOK and MPV17, and also POLG, which impair maintenance of the mitochondrial genome
Typically presents in the first weeks to months of life with cholestasis, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, and lactic acidosis progressing to liver failure
Neurological features include hypotonia, developmental delay, nystagmus, and, in some forms, a hepatocerebral phenotype with encephalopathy
Diagnosis relies on demonstrating reduced mitochondrial DNA content in liver tissue and reduced respiratory chain enzyme activity
A raised blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate supports a mitochondrial cause
Management is supportive; liver transplantation is controversial because of extrahepatic (neurological) disease and must be considered case by case
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes result from defects in nuclear genes that maintain the mitochondrial genome or supply deoxyribonucleotides for its replication. Mutations in DGUOK (deoxyguanosine kinase) disturb the mitochondrial nucleotide pool, MPV17 encodes an inner-membrane protein needed for genome maintenance, and POLG encodes the mitochondrial DNA polymerase. The resulting depletion of mitochondrial DNA cripples oxidative phosphorylation in high-demand tissues, producing early hepatocellular failure with cholestasis, hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis, together with progressive neurological dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Other respiratory chain disorders and Alpers syndrome (POLG)
additionalInvestigations: Blood lactate, lactate/pyruvate ratio, and glucose
Liver function tests, serum bile acids, and coagulation profile
Liver biopsy with quantitative mitochondrial DNA content
Respiratory chain enzyme analysis in liver or muscle
Brain MRI and cerebrospinal fluid lactate where encephalopathy is present
Gene panel testing including DGUOK, MPV17, and POLG
redFlags: Acute infantile liver failure with coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia
Progressive encephalopathy or intractable seizures (especially POLG)
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor, with many infants dying of liver failure or neurological disease in the first years of life; liver transplantation may help isolated hepatic forms but does not address neurological involvement and carries a worse outcome when extrahepatic disease is present.
pitfalls: Proceeding to liver transplantation without assessing for significant neurological involvement
Missing lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia as pointers to a mitochondrial cause
Confusing the picture with neonatal haemochromatosis or metabolic liver disease
Using sodium valproate in suspected POLG disease, which can precipitate liver failure
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
management: No specific cure; supportive management of hepatic failure with correction of coagulopathy, treatment of hypoglycaemia by regular feeding and intravenous dextrose, and relief of cholestasis
Nutritional support to prevent catabolism, with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation in cholestasis
Treat lactic acidosis and metabolic decompensation with intravenous dextrose and fluids
Avoid hepatotoxic and mitochondrial-toxic drugs, particularly sodium valproate, which can precipitate fatal liver failure especially in POLG-related disease
Liver transplantation considered for isolated hepatic disease but weighed carefully, as it does not correct neurological involvement and outcomes are worse with extrahepatic disease
Neurological monitoring with symptomatic care such as anticonvulsants and developmental support for the hepatocerebral phenotype
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with carrier testing and prenatal options for the family
